\chapter{Answering, Meeting, and Three Ways to Play}
\label{ch:pt-answering-meeting-playing}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I answer and meet in Portuguese, split meeting between encontrar and conhecer, and choose among the three verbs Portuguese uses for playing — jogar, brincar and tocar.}

The chapter's last lesson closes the set: after the three play verbs the reader produces all five first-person forms in one run - respondo, encontro, jogo, brinco, toco - chooses jogar, brincar or tocar by the kind of playing, and names brincar as the one root of the three that is genuinely unsettled.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[responder]{responder — answering, and a promise given back}

\label{lesson:PT-C22-responder}



\begin{quote}
A chapter of verbs for dealing with other people opens with the one this book has been missing. You have been able to ask since the last chapter. Now you can answer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: A plain -er verb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{respondo} & nós \textbf{respondemos} \\
tu \textbf{respondes} & vocês/eles \textbf{respondem} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{responde} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Responder} is regular all the way through — an ordinary \emph{-er} verb, the same shape as the writing and reading verbs you already conjugate. It pairs with \emph{perguntar} exactly as English \textquotedblleft{}answer\textquotedblright{} pairs with \textquotedblleft{}ask\textquotedblright{}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Pergunto e tu respondes.} — \textquotedblleft{}I ask and you answer.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Respondo que compro o pão.} — \textquotedblleft{}I answer that I am buying the bread.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The most everyday answer of all is one you have had since the third chapter. Asked \textbf{Como se chama?}, you \emph{respond}: \textbf{Chamo-me…}, and then \textbf{muito prazer}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{responder} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{respondēre}}: \emph{re-}, \textquotedblleft{}back,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{\textbf{spondēre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to pledge, to promise solemnly.\textquotedblright{} A Roman answer was not information handed over — it was a \textbf{promise returned}. Somebody pledged, and you pledged back.

That old weight is still on the English side of the family. \textbf{Respond} and \textbf{response} are the plain ones, but a \textbf{responsible} person is one who can be called on to answer, and to be \textbf{despondent} is to have given the pledge away. A \textbf{sponsor} is literally one who pledges for you — and a \textbf{spouse} is \emph{spōnsus}, \textquotedblleft{}the one who has been promised.\textquotedblright{}

Set that against the verb it answers. \textbf{Perguntar} came from \emph{percontārī}, from \emph{contus}, a boatman's pole: to ask was to sound the depth of the water in front of you. So Portuguese probes with a pole and pledges back with a promise.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}respondo, respondes, responde, respondemos, respondem\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Pergunto e tu respondes\textquotedblright{}
  \item answering the oldest question — \textquotedblleft{}Chamo-me… muito prazer\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Respondo que compro o pão\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pledging family — \textquotedblleft{}sponsor · spouse · responsible\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the present of \emph{responder}. (\textbf{Respondo, respondes, responde, respondemos, respondem}.) What did \emph{spondēre} mean, and which English word for a married person comes from it? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{pledge}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{\textbf{spouse}}, \emph{spōnsus}.) Now answer \emph{Como se chama?} aloud. (\emph{\textbf{Chamo-me…}}, then \emph{\textbf{muito prazer}}.) What was the pole in \emph{perguntar}? (\emph{Contus} — asking as \textbf{sounding the depth}.) And is \emph{comprar} related to \emph{compare}? (\textbf{No} — \emph{comprar} comes from \emph{parāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to make ready.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[encontrar]{encontrar — to find}

\label{lesson:PT-C22-encontrar}



\begin{quote}
Today \textbf{encontrar} has one job: “to find.”
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The present tense}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
eu \textbf{encontro} & nós \textbf{encontramos} \\
tu \textbf{encontras} & vocês/eles \textbf{encontram} \\
ele/ela/você \textbf{encontra} &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Encontro o livro.} — I find the book. \textbf{Encontramos o café.} — We find the café.
\end{quote}

Keep the object directly after the verb, as in English.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Encontrar} grew from \emph{in} plus Latin \emph{\textbf{contrā}}, “facing” or “opposite.” To find something is to come face to face with it. English \textbf{encounter} belongs to the same family.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{encontro, encontras, encontra, encontramos, encontram}
  \item “I find the book” — \textbf{Encontro o livro.}
  \item “We find the café” — \textbf{Encontramos o café.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say “I find.” (\textbf{Encontro.}) Say “We find the café.” (\textbf{Encontramos o café.}) Which English word shares the same family? (\textbf{Encounter.}) Next, \textbf{encontrar} will gain one social meaning.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[encontrar-se]{encontrar-se — to meet up}

\label{lesson:PT-C22-encontrar-meet}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{encontrar}, “to find.” With people, it can also describe meeting up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Make one plan}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Encontramo-nos no sábado ao meio-dia.} — We are meeting on Saturday at midday.
\end{quote}

The little \textbf{nos} means “each other.” In much of Portugal it commonly attaches after the verb as shown. In Brazil, \textbf{nós nos encontramos} is more usual.

For a first introduction, keep using the \textbf{conhecer} family you already know: \textbf{Conheci o Pedro}, “I met Pedro for the first time.” Today’s \textbf{encontrar-se} is for meeting up.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{Encontramo-nos no sábado.}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{Nós nos encontramos no sábado.}
  \item \emph{Choose:} A first introduction uses \textbf{encontrar} or \textbf{conhecer}? (\textbf{Conhecer.})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say “We are meeting on Saturday” in the Portugal pattern. (\textbf{Encontramo-nos no sábado.}) Which pattern is common in Brazil? (\textbf{Nós nos encontramos.}) Which verb handles a first introduction? (\textbf{Conhecer.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jogar / brincar / tocar]{jogar / brincar / tocar — the three ways to play}

\label{lesson:PT-C22-jogar-brincar-tocar}



\begin{quote}
English plays chess, plays in the garden and plays the piano with one verb. Portuguese has three, and will not let you swap them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Which play is which}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{\textbf{jogar} — a game} & \textbf{\textbf{brincar} — a child, a joke} & \textbf{\textbf{tocar} — an instrument} \\
\midrule
\textbf{jogo, jogas, joga} & \textbf{brinco, brincas, brinca} & \textbf{toco, tocas, toca} \\
Jogo futebol. & O meu irmão brinca. & Toco piano. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All three are ordinary \emph{-ar} verbs, endings exactly as in \emph{falar}, \emph{morar} and \emph{trabalhar}. The work is choosing.

\textbf{Jogar} is a game with rules and a winner. \textbf{Brincar} is free play — a child with a toy, and from there joking, so \emph{brincar com} someone is to tease them. \textbf{Tocar} is an instrument. \emph{Brincar} is the one English cannot match: \textquotedblleft{}play\textquotedblright{} is too wide, \textquotedblleft{}mess about\textquotedblright{} too dismissive.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Two coasts, one preposition apart}]
Portugal commonly puts an \emph{a} after \emph{jogar}: \textbf{jogar à bola}, \textbf{jogar às cartas}. Brazil, and northern Portugal, take the thing straight: \textbf{jogar bola}.

\emph{Tocar} also keeps its plainer meaning, \textbf{to touch}. You touch with a \textbf{mão} — and a piano wants \textbf{as duas mãos}, \emph{duas} not \emph{dois}, because \emph{mão} is feminine.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jogar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{\textbf{iocārī}}, \textquotedblleft{}to jest,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{iocus}, \textquotedblleft{}a joke\textquotedblright{} $\to$ English \textbf{joke}, \textbf{jocular}, and \textbf{juggler}, a Latin \emph{ioculātor} or jester. Portuguese plays its games with the Latin word for a gag.

\textbf{tocar} $\leftarrow$ Vulgar Latin \emph{\textbf{toccāre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to knock, to strike,\textquotedblright{} most likely an imitation of the sound. Old French carried it into English as \textbf{touch} — a blow at its lightest is a touch. The striking sense stayed with music: a \textbf{toccata}, a \textbf{tocsin} or alarm bell. You \emph{tocar} an instrument because you strike it.

\textbf{brincar} is the honest gap. The leading account runs through \textbf{brinco}, today \textquotedblleft{}an earring,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \emph{vinculum}, \textquotedblleft{}a bond\textquotedblright{} — a bound ornament, then a trinket, then playing with trinkets. A Germanic word for gleaming is the rival, and neither is settled. \emph{Vinculum} survives plainly as \textbf{vínculo}, \textquotedblleft{}a bond.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole chapter — \textquotedblleft{}respondo, encontro, jogo, brinco, toco\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Jogo futebol\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}Toco piano\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}O meu irmão brinca\textquotedblright{}
  \item with both hands — \textquotedblleft{}a mão, as duas mãos\textquotedblright{}
  \item the striking family — \textquotedblleft{}tocar · touch · toccata\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the verb for a sport, the one for a child, the one for a piano. (\emph{\textbf{Jogar}}; \emph{\textbf{brincar}}; \emph{\textbf{tocar}}.) Give this chapter's five \emph{eu} forms. (\textbf{Respondo, encontro, jogo, brinco, toco}.) Which of the three has no settled root? (\emph{\textbf{Brincar}}.) What did \emph{toccāre} mean, and which English word is it? (\textquotedblleft{}To \textbf{strike}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{\textbf{touch}}.) Why \emph{as duas mãos}? (\emph{Mão} is \textbf{feminine}.) And which verb meets a person for the first time? (\emph{\textbf{Conhecer}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
